content.title: From soil to jobs: how the food sector can become an engine of green growth
content.description: The need for greater domestic supply capacity and preparedness is growing rapidly, as are demands to reduce climate and environmental impact. By stepping up the green transition, Sweden can produce more food, strengthen the sector's competitiveness and resilience, and create tens of thousands of new jobs.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces major challenges in food supply, preparedness, climate and competitiveness – but also major opportunities. In the report Grön uppväxling, Swedish farmers and food producers present a shared evidence base and a concrete roadmap for increasing Swedish food and beverage production while reducing climate impact and strengthening biodiversity.

The seminar discusses how Sweden can take greater responsibility for its own and Europe's food supply, the conditions needed to increase production, how tens of thousands of new jobs can be created, and how growth in agriculture and the food industry can be combined with high environmental and climate ambitions.

The discussion starts from the enormous growth potential in Sweden's primary and food production, and the political, economic and structural changes needed to enable a green scale-up.

content.description: Six in ten Swedes were exposed to criminal advertisements last year. content.title: How do we create long-term conditions for building housing for older people?
content.description: Sweden faces a sharp increase in its older population, particularly those over 80, while access to secure housing is declining. The sector wants to contribute, but projects are financially challenging without investment support. How can we meet the needs, with or without new support?
content.extendedDescription:
There are three reasons why Sweden faces a housing crisis for older people.

• Construction of new care homes and other housing for older people has not kept pace with needs, despite a sharp rise in the number of people over 80.

• Municipalities cannot finance the necessary investments alone. General government grants are crucial to running elder care but are neither intended nor sufficient for new construction.

• Investment support for housing for older people has been abolished.

Sweden faces a choice. Municipal investment needs are growing, the population is ageing and more older people remain in homes not adapted to tomorrow's needs. The question is not whether to act, but how. Should municipalities be left to bear the investments alone? Is it reasonable for older people to be forced to remain in homes that limit their safety and quality of life? Or must the state take greater responsibility?

This seminar discusses ways forward and solutions that work.
content.subject: Older people
speakerTitles: Head of Business Development, Residential Elder Care

content.title: What role does energy efficiency play in a digitalised, AI-driven society?
content.description: The transition and digitalisation have created a gap between organisations that understand and want to contribute to the transition and those lacking ambition, tools or resources. Society must work towards the same goal in this effort.
content.extendedDescription:
The panel discusses how leadership needs to develop to meet the technological transition and the growing demands that digitalisation, AI and sustainability targets place on organisations today.

The focus is on the leadership required, coordination and the ability to drive change forward.
Many projects lose momentum today, not because of a lack of ambition, but because responsibility, communication and a shared overview are not maintained throughout the process.
The discussion also explores how AI and digitalisation can improve decision support and cooperation to achieve ‘Netto-=’ buildings, while organisations need to develop their working methods and leadership to fully harness technology's opportunities. How does Sweden differ from the rest of the world, and what can we learn from other countries?

content.title: Can local economies be the answer to the climate crisis, inequality and vulnerable communities?
content.description: The globalized economic system has long been promised as a path to prosperity and efficiency — but the result has been ever increasing climate emissions, fragile supply chains and growing gaps between people. Now, a movement is growing for building new economies on a human scale.
content.extendedDescription:
On June 23, two voices from the international localization movement will come to Almedalen to share concrete solutions and inspiring examples. They will talk about their work to shed light on one of the least discussed but most influential drivers behind this development: free trade agreements and the so-called ISDS (Investor-State Dispute Settlement) mechanisms, which give multinational companies the right to sue states when political decisions threaten their expected profits. This has in practice made it more difficult for countries to pursue active climate policies, protect local markets and safeguard the interests of their citizens.

Fatima Osman Abdalla, active in Real Economy, and Henry Coleman from Local Futures — the organization founded by Right Livelihood Award recipient Helena Norberg-Hodge — meet for a conversation about economies on a human scale, beyond global corporate capitalism.

content.title: How can we secure future skills in Sweden's vital industries?
content.description: Industries that underpin Swedish society face a skills crisis, while few people are choosing to enter them. How can we attract young people to careers in agriculture, forestry or the countryside?
content.extendedDescription:
A changing climate and increasing geopolitical tensions call for stronger Swedish preparedness. We need to produce more food with a smaller climate footprint, balance forests' role as both carbon sinks and sources of raw materials, and protect biodiversity. The need for expertise in the green industries has never been greater. Yet few people apply to the educational programmes that hold the solutions. Is this a matter of image, a gap in knowledge, or the complex conflicts between objectives that young people are expected to navigate today?

Join a breakfast discussion in which young and slightly less young people discuss the supply of skills in the green industries. We begin with a crash course in the challenges ahead, followed by a panel discussion in which tomorrow's decision-makers give their views. What is needed to encourage young people to pursue careers as, for example, agronomists, horticultural scientists or professional foresters? We finish with mingling and networking with students, decision-makers and those of us passionate about green issues.

content.title: How should we assess evidence in labour market policy?
content.description: How robust is the evidence underpinning the government's shift in labour market policy – and what happens when it turns out to rest on uncertain methodological choices? When key evaluations are questioned, the knowledge base of labour market policy comes under scrutiny.
content.extendedDescription: IFAU's impact evaluation of Rusta och matcha has had considerable influence and informed political decisions to reduce the role of independent job-matching providers. But a replication of the study using the same data, conducted by Svenskt Näringsliv, shows that its conclusions are not robust. In practice, this means political decisions may have been based on fragile evidence. A possible consequence is a reassessment of matching services, risking poorer support for jobseekers and a less effective matching system. The question is therefore not just what the findings show, but how we ensure they are reliable before translating them into policy. The panel discusses the political consequences of IFAU's report, evaluation agencies' responsibility for presenting findings in policy reports, how to ensure evaluations actually measure what we think they measure, and what is at stake for unemployed people, employers and the matching system when evidence is weak.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.description: How can we build a democracy in which everyone is heard and decisions are based on our shared collective will rather than well-resourced special interests?
content.extendedDescription:
A functioning democracy depends on all voices having an equal opportunity to be heard. Yet we know this is not the reality: instead, those with the strongest financial resources are usually heard most, often at the expense of the planet, our health, facts and our rights.

We invite you to a conversation about how we can build a democracy in which everyone is heard and decisions are based on our shared collective will rather than well-resourced special interests.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Policy instruments that work in practice – how do we achieve the transition without weakening competitiveness?
content.description: Sweden's climate targets require a rapid transition in the transport sector, while road transport remains essential to trade, industry and supplies. The question is not only which policy instruments are introduced, but how they are designed to work in practice for hauliers and transport buyers.
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, we discuss how policy instruments can contribute to both lower emissions and stronger competitiveness. What is needed to create long-term, predictable conditions that enable investment? How do we avoid stop-start policies that slow progress?

We particularly highlight HVO and other biofuels as a necessary option for rapidly reducing emissions from the existing vehicle fleet while electrification and other new technologies are developed.

Join a discussion about how to create policies that deliver climate benefits, security and functioning transport, and enable companies to transition while strengthening competitiveness.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: The technology exists and the trucks are running – why is hydrogen still seen as science fiction?
content.description: Hydrogen for transport is still often portrayed as a distant prospect. Yet heavy hydrogen-powered trucks already operate in Sweden, filling stations stretch from Malmö to northern Sweden, and new production facilities are being built. What is actually true about hydrogen mobility in 2026?
content.extendedDescription:
Hydrogen for transport is still often portrayed as a distant prospect, a future project that might arrive later. Yet heavy hydrogen-powered trucks already operate in Sweden, filling stations stretch from Malmö to northern Sweden, and new production facilities are being built at prices approaching those of other fossil-free alternatives.
So why do some people still seem to think hydrogen is like Santa Claus: something they enjoy discussing but do not really believe exists?
During the seminar, Hydri brings together transport, logistics and energy stakeholders to discuss real experience, business perspectives and a straightforward question: what is actually true about hydrogen mobility in 2026, and what persists as outdated beliefs, misunderstandings or outright lies?
We discuss how far development has progressed, the remaining barriers and when hydrogen becomes a business rather than just a pilot project.
The seminar concludes with a panel discussion and audience questions. Do not expect complete agreement. That makes it much more interesting.

content.title: Does Sweden's energy transition risk stalling?
content.description: During the year, electricity producers have encountered resistance in trying to obtain judicial review of grid charge issues through regulatory supervision.
content.extendedDescription:
Last year's panel organised by Svensk Vindkraft discussed the unequal situation for feed-in customers (electricity producers) in Sweden compared with the rest of the EU. A particular question was whether the then-new grid tariff rules were EU-compatible. These regulations from Energimarknadsinspektionen (EIFS 2022:1) are now to be repealed by 30 June 2026 at the latest. What comes next is unclear.

The question Svensk Vindkraft wants to highlight this year is whether it is almost time for an electricity producers' revolt. Does Sweden's energy transition risk stalling if producers' costs become significantly higher than elsewhere in the EU?

content.title: The menopause effect: the billions lost in healthcare and at work
content.description: Although most women experience menopausal symptoms at some point, organisations lack strategic planning and workplace health measures to address them. Greater knowledge can give more women better health, enable continued full participation in working life and improve well-being.
content.extendedDescription:
Although most women experience menopausal symptoms at some point, the issue is almost absent from organisations' strategic planning and workplace health efforts. Lack of knowledge also leads to women being mistreated or dismissed, contributing, alongside other factors, to higher sick leave rates among women over 45 than among men.

Making menopause a strategic workplace health issue can help retain invaluable expertise and drive future growth and health.

Join a conversation between medical experts, business and society. During Almedalsveckan 2026, we challenge stigma and advance work on hormonal health, other treatments and menopause. We discuss current research and practical solutions that strengthen women's health and minimise hidden production losses currently costing Swedish companies billions through sick leave and reduced work performance.

The discussion continues in smaller conversations with experts. More speakers will be announced.

content.title: Pharmacist-supplied medicines – opportunities, responsibilities and the way forward
content.description: The Tidö Agreement announces a new category of non-prescription medicines that pharmacies may sell following individual advice from a pharmacist. The reform aims to ease pressure on healthcare and strengthen conditions for prevention and informed self-care.
content.extendedDescription:
Similar models have long been established in countries such as Norway and the United Kingdom, with documented positive results.
At the time of this seminar, the reform is at a decisive stage. We meet, regardless of the bill's position in the decision-making process, to analyse the conditions for successful implementation and the changes the reform brings to pharmacies, industry and the healthcare system.

Topics include:
How should successful introduction of pharmacist-supplied medicines be designed, and what are the critical success factors?
What does the reform require of pharmaceutical companies, pharmacies and other stakeholders to achieve its intended effect?
How can pharmacies' role in preventive healthcare be strengthened and clarified within the new category?

We welcome decision-makers, industry representatives and experts to discuss a reform with the potential to change Swedish medicine supply and self-care over the long term.

content.title: Mental health among young people with diabetes
content.description: Living with type 1 diabetes affects both physical and mental health. Many young people with diabetes feel stress, worry and pressure from constantly having to manage their condition. This can lead to anxiety, low mood and feelings of exclusion, making mental health an important issue for society.
content.extendedDescription:
Living with type 1 diabetes affects not only the body but also mental health. Many young people describe stress, worry, tiredness and the feeling of always having to think about blood sugar, insulin and food. It is common to feel different, frustrated or overwhelmed at times.

Ung diabetes has therefore produced the discussion booklet ‘How are you? Practical tips for conversations about mental health and diabetes’. The booklet aims to create a sense of safety and open up important conversations about the mental wellbeing of young people with type 1 diabetes. Its goal is to reduce stigma, increase understanding and show that no one needs to carry their feelings alone.

Mental wellbeing needs more attention in diabetes care. The question ‘How are you?’ must be just as important as ‘What is your HbA1c?’ during a visit to the diabetes clinic.

Mental health is an important part of diabetes care, and talking about how you feel can make a big difference.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Exercise on prescription – a natural part of today's prostate cancer treatment and rehabilitation?
content.description: Receiving a prostate cancer diagnosis and undergoing treatment often affect both the body and energy levels. Particularly during hormone therapy, side effects such as reduced muscle mass, increased body fat, fatigue and osteoporosis can make people feel weaker over time. Regular exercise makes a difference.
content.extendedDescription:
Regular physical activity can help counteract adverse effects of prostate cancer treatment and contribute to better quality of life.

Research and healthcare rehabilitation recommendations indicate that exercise is not merely 'good to do' – it can actively contribute to recovery. A combination of aerobic and strength training is often particularly valuable for maintaining strength, balance and endurance. For many, a simple start may be enough: regular walks, lighter strength exercises at home and gradually increasing intensity.

In this discussion, we explore examples where exercise has made a major difference to individual patients in concrete projects in which Prostatacancerförbundet has made high-intensity training available to men undergoing prostate cancer treatment in region Skåne. Meanwhile, exciting research into the subject is under way at Gymnastik och idrottshögskolan, GIH, in Stockholm.

You can stay after the event to speak with the participants.

content.title: Does democracy die in the heat?
content.description: Is the climate crisis a crisis of democracy? What roles do disinformation and polarisation play in our ability to make the transition? The climate crisis demands long-term decisions, while politics is often governed by short electoral terms and public opinion. How does this affect the ability to maintain ambitious climate policy?
content.extendedDescription:
The climate crisis challenges democracy's fundamental logic. Long-term, complex risks must be managed within political systems characterised by short electoral terms and strong conflicts of interest. Meanwhile, climate issues are increasingly used to undermine trust in science, the media and democratic institutions.

This discussion describes how the climate crisis can contribute to democratic decline and create space for authoritarian forces, making both climate policy and democratic decision-making more difficult.

The climate debate has also become increasingly polarised, with trust in the media and research undermined by hate, threats and organised denial.

We also discuss ways forward that can strengthen democracy's ability to manage the transition.

content.title: AI data centres and energy: a Swedish business opportunity?
content.description: Data centres require electricity, capacity and fast permitting. The question is where investment will go. With the right ground rules, AI could become Sweden's greatest investment and employment opportunity.
content.extendedDescription:
AI development is moving at breakneck speed, and its use is becoming a decisive factor in Sweden's competitiveness. But AI has a physical reality: behind every model and service are data centres requiring large amounts of electricity, connection capacity in record time and a robust power system. The question is not whether this infrastructure will be built, but where. Sweden may be facing its greatest external investment opportunity ever. But the conditions must be right, or investment, skills and innovation could go elsewhere.

At this seminar, we bring together participants from several parts of the AI value chain to discuss the ground rules needed both to accelerate expansion and maximise benefits for Sweden. As Europe electrifies, seeks greater energy independence and tries to catch up in AI, energy is once again central. Designed correctly, this is an opportunity to equip Sweden with major investments in data centres and energy infrastructure and create thousands of jobs.

content.title: Who will take responsibility for making academic ATMP treatments available when industry steps back?
content.description: More academically developed cell and gene therapies are showing promising results for small patient groups, while industry withdraws from unprofitable ATMP treatments. Swedish university hospitals have the capacity, but current regulations are insufficient. Are new routes to implementation needed?
content.extendedDescription:
An increasing number of academically developed cell and gene therapies are undergoing clinical trials with promising results in diseases affecting small patient populations. At the same time, industry is discontinuing effective ATMPs for small patient populations where they are not financially or commercially viable. Swedish university hospitals have both the expertise and capacity to collaborate on production and clinical treatment, but clear routes to offering these treatments are lacking: neither commercial marketing authorisation nor the hospital exemption is a suitable way forward. Do we need to consider new routes for introducing treatments of academic origin, given how they challenge current systems?

PROGRAMME
Interview: CAR T treatment from a patient's perspective, Göran Eriksson, cancer-free after 25 years.
Panel discussion with public authorities, politicians and experts.

content.title: Voters' views on snus, e-cigarettes and nicotine – how do politicians respond?
content.description: We know a great deal about how Swedes use snus, e-cigarettes and nicotine, but less about their knowledge, risk perceptions and attitudes towards these products. Ahead of the election, it is important to understand how well party positions reflect voters' views on public health, individual freedom and EU influence.
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar presents Snusbarometern, a new opinion survey aiming to fill gaps in knowledge about Swedes' attitudes towards snus, e-cigarettes and different nicotine products. The survey examines views on risks, the role of snus in quitting smoking, young people's use and how much power the EU should have over taxes and regulations.

Drawing on the survey, we invite you to a political discussion in which the panel reacts to, is challenged by and reflects on what public opinion actually shows. How can better knowledge of Swedes' views on snus, e-cigarettes and nicotine contribute to better-targeted decisions on public health, individual freedom and Sweden's position in EU negotiations?

content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

content.title: No more guesswork — time for mandatory age verification when buying nicotine?
content.description: Despite a strict age limit of 18, nicotine and tobacco are still sold in shops to minors across the country. After years of training initiatives, shops' actual compliance with age checks remains inadequate. When too few people dare to ask about age, is a change in the law needed?
content.extendedDescription:
A new Ipsos survey shows that minors across the country often succeed in buying nicotine and tobacco products in shops. Years of proactive work involving internal compliance programmes, training and technical solutions have not been enough to reverse the trend.

This seminar brings together representatives from industry, public authorities and politics to jointly identify solutions that can break the trend once and for all. It begins with a presentation of the findings from Ipsos's latest survey of retail sales to minors.

Is it time to move from responsibility at cashier level to statutory, mandatory age verification for nicotine purchases, to reduce hesitation, errors of judgement and social pressure at the checkout?
content.subject: Children/young people
speakerTitles: Deputy Mayor for Social Affairs and Public Safety

content.title: Older but not old
content.description: More than 2 million Swedes have reached what we call retirement age. They are individuals with very different lives, motivations and dreams, yet they are often portrayed stereotypically and as passive members of society. Why?
content.extendedDescription:
In Sweden, more than two million people have reached what we call retirement age. They are often depicted stereotypically and portrayed as passive members of society.

Photographer Evelina Carborn wants to help change that image with the exhibition Äldre men inte gammal. It portrays people with very different lives, motivations and dreams. Many may be older, but they are far from old – and share the view that the general image of “older people” is simplistic and outdated.

The exhibition can be seen throughout Almedalsveckan on Donnersgatan, halfway between Almedalsparken and Almedalsbiblioteket. Guided tours are also offered on Wednesday and Thursday.

content.title: Sustainability through quality-assured measurement, traceability and digital product passports in the forest industry
content.description: We want to build more with wood – but how do we know it is actually sustainable? When data follows materials from forest to reuse, digital product passports can provide evidence, not just claims, about origin, processing, climate impact, quality and reusability.
content.extendedDescription:
Wood is a key material in the transition, but sustainability cannot rest on assumptions. It must be demonstrated, verified and improved. Large amounts of data are collected along the forest value chain today, but information often remains trapped in separate systems.
You will hear a presentation with examples from technology and a demonstrator. We show how traceability methods can connect data sources and establish relationships between measurements that otherwise remain isolated islands of data. We introduce ENTER, a research project developing a demonstrator for a digital value chain from forests and sawmills to building systems, construction, management and reuse, using real data and connected APIs.
Imagine a plank had eyes. What would it see along the way? The digital process declaration collects actual measurements – the product's ACTUAL values. The digital product passport brings together standards, certifications and product specifications – its REQUIRED values. Together, they provide a basis for sustainability, improvement and competitiveness.

content.title: Feminism and men's violence against women – where do the parties stand?
content.description: Where do the parties stand on men's violence against women, surrogacy and abortion? How far are they willing to go to reduce women's and girls' vulnerability in pornography and prostitution?
content.extendedDescription:
An election takes place in September, with much discussion of healthcare, law and order and schools. Men's violence against women rarely receives much attention in election debates. Yet a recent Novus survey shows that 63 per cent of the population consider it important to have a women's or girls' support service near where they live. Fully 81 per cent believe children should have the right to accompany a mother experiencing violence if she is placed in protected accommodation,* despite new reforms making this harder.

This election debate focuses wholeheartedly on feminist issues, particularly men's violence against women. Topics include honour-based violence, prostitution, pornography, surrogacy, abortion, women's and girls' support services and protected accommodation.

Afterwards, there will be mingling with drinks and snacks while supplies last.

*Novus conducted the survey in week 17 of 2026 for Roks, using online interviews with a randomly recruited Swedish panel. A total of 1,003 people aged 18-84 participated.

content.title: Children's summit and student citizens' assembly — engaging children and young people in local democracy
content.description: What does practical work on democracy look like in preschools and schools? We are seeing a trend in which fewer young people regard democracy as the best way to govern a country, while more consider a strong leader or expert a better alternative.
content.extendedDescription:
How can we build strong support for democracy in preschools and schools? By Almedalsveckan, the student citizens' assembly will have met twice. Karlstads kommun was the first municipality in the country to launch a student citizens' assembly for the climate. This democracy project aims to engage children and young people in climate and environmental issues and build confidence in the future and capacity to act by enabling real influence on local democracy.

In autumn 2022, pupils in Karlstads kommun's compulsory schools developed 967 concrete proposals. Of the final 67 proposals submitted to politicians, many have been approved for implementation. One proposal approved by the Children and Youth Committee was to create a permanent student citizens' assembly. This year, we developed the assembly into a children's summit during Barnrättsdagarna, on the theme of social sustainability.

content.title: What does failure at school cost?
content.description: Every year, tens of thousands of pupils are failed by the Swedish school system. This costs both individuals and society dearly. What does educational failure cost, and what needs to be done so more pupils succeed at school?
content.extendedDescription: Pupils failing at school has major consequences for individuals and society as a whole. In collaboration with economist Ingvar Nilsson and behavioural scientist Eva Nilsson, Sveriges Lärare has made new calculations of the cost of educational failure. A clue: considerably more than preventing it would have cost. Welcome to a seminar where we present the figures and discuss what needs to be done.

content.title: Why are companies overlooking one of the world's largest minority groups?
content.description: People with disabilities make up one of the world's largest minority groups, yet remain invisible in much business communication and strategy. How can business value, representation and inclusion create benefits for both society and business?
content.extendedDescription:
People with disabilities make up one of the world's largest minority groups. Around 16 per cent of the global population lives with some form of disability, and the group represents significant economic and social influence. Globally, its combined disposable income is estimated at almost USD 2 trillion annually. Yet people with disabilities remain heavily underrepresented in corporate strategies, marketing and communications.

In Sweden, around 12 per cent of the working-age population has a disability, while the employment rate is considerably lower among people with reduced work capacity.

During the seminar, American researcher Edward Timke presents current research on disability in communication and visibility in society. This is followed by a discussion about business value, inclusion, representation and how companies and society can together contribute to real change.

content.title: Step into Matoteket 2035: the lunch where tomorrow's teaching has already begun
content.description: School meals reach almost every Swedish pupil daily and offer major opportunities to strengthen learning, health, sustainable development and community. What if they had a clearer educational role? How could that enrich the school day, and which decisions would enable it?
content.extendedDescription:
In this interactive future experience, participants enter ‘Matoteket’ in 2035, an interdisciplinary learning environment where lunch and teaching form a natural part of the school day.

During 45 minutes, visitors join a simulated lunch lesson using the meal as an educational tool. The experience draws on future scenarios and policy proposals developed within Policylabbet Offentlig Måltid, a Vinnova-funded collaboration between research, the public sector and civil society within the Mission Matmiljö and PUSH innovation platforms.

It concludes with a short panel on opportunities, barriers and policy changes needed for school meals to become an established learning environment in tomorrow's schools.

content.title: Skills and education without geographical barriers — how do we reach the whole country?
content.description: Skills shortages affect both business competitiveness and the quality of welfare. How can higher education, distance learning and local learning centres strengthen skills supply and create opportunities for growth throughout Sweden, including far from university campuses?
content.extendedDescription:
Access to the right skills is crucial to Sweden's competitiveness, welfare and regional development. Yet many employers face major recruitment challenges, particularly in smaller municipalities and areas far from universities and university colleges. How can education become more accessible and contribute to development nationwide?

The seminar discusses current and future skills and education needs, and the solutions required for more people to access higher education regardless of where they live.

The seminar is organised by Akademi Norr and Lapplands Kommunalförbund with support from Kompetensarena Norrbotten. The project works to strengthen strategic skills supply in Norrbotten through better evidence, cooperation and support structures for municipalities and employers.

content.title: Violence, custody and contact – have the legislative changes helped?
content.description: How have recent legislative changes affected whether violent fathers are granted custody and contact with their children? And how are pseudoscientific theories used in custody cases?
content.extendedDescription:
Roks presents a new edition of its report Våld och vårdnad (Eva Diesen, 2026), examining how violence, risk assessments and parental responsibility are handled in Swedish custody disputes. The aim is to highlight how courts apply current law in cases concerning custody, residence and contact where allegations of violence arise, and to analyse the legal and practical consequences for children and parents.

The report has been updated with legislation and case law through 2026.
Particular emphasis is placed on developments following the legislative changes that took effect in 2025, intended to strengthen protection for children and parents exposed to violence.

We ask: has the new legislation had an effect? Is violence considered when deciding custody, residence and contact? And how does the justice system view arguments about parental influence, known as parental alienation?

content.title: Nordic profits: time for a harmonised fund market
content.description: A strong market for savings and investment is crucial for competitiveness and growth. The Nordic capital markets are prominent but too small and nationally focused. Differences in legal form, marketing and taxation, for example, obstruct cross-border fund trading.
content.extendedDescription:
As EU regulations are reformed and implemented, Nordic finance ministries and supervisory authorities need to collaborate. The Nordic region has the capital, expertise and trust to be a leading European market for savings and asset management, but is held back by national arrangements and a lack of coordination.

What can the Nordic countries gain by taking joint steps forward, and what needs to be done to achieve a more integrated capital market?

What is needed to create better conditions for administering, distributing and managing funds efficiently across the Nordic region? Which regulations or processes are most important to harmonise? What effect would a common market have on access to capital in Sweden and the Nordic region? How can we become a stronger collective voice in the EU while creating a more competitive offering for savers and investors?

content.title: From need to reality: why does defence innovation get stuck in Sweden?
content.description: Needs-driven innovation has become a mantra in defence. In practice, it risks becoming both narrow and slow. When needs are defined in advance, often by major players with established methods, we risk missing the unexpected: disruptive solutions from small, agile companies.
content.extendedDescription:
Needs-driven innovation has become a mantra in defence. In practice, however, it risks becoming both narrow and slow. When needs are defined in advance, often by large organisations with established methods, we risk missing the unexpected: disruptive solutions from small, agile companies. Meanwhile, many innovative companies cannot enter the defence sector. They do not know whom to approach, how procurement works or how to connect with major prime contractors. Entry routes are unclear. How can we create a defence innovation system that is both needs-driven and open to the unexpected?

• What do we actually mean by needs-driven innovation in defence?
• When does being guided by needs become an obstacle to innovation?
• What is needed for small companies to genuinely work with the defence sector?
• How can prime contractors and startups collaborate without getting stuck in processes?
• Who takes responsibility for the interface between the public sector, prime contractors and startups?

content.title: Over-indebtedness among young people: a turnaround in sight?
content.description: After years of increasing over-indebtedness among people aged 18–34, a turnaround may be in sight. Forecasts suggest that the number of people in debt will fall in 2026. Yet many young people still face serious debt problems. Are we moving towards more sustainable borrowing, and what is driving the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
After several years of increasing over-indebtedness among people aged 18–34, statistics released in 2025 showed signs of a possible turnaround. Kronofogden's forecasts suggest that the number of people in debt will fall in 2026. Yet many young people still face serious debt problems.

Are we moving towards more sustainable borrowing among young people, and if so, what is driving the change? What is needed for a turnaround to happen and for the trend to continue towards fewer young people experiencing payment difficulties?

The seminar and discussion draw on the latest knowledge as we seek answers to these important questions. We also discuss why young adults take on debt, with the myth of ‘Lyxfällan’-style behaviour challenged by both experts and young people's own accounts of financial vulnerability.

The panel includes experts from KTH, Liberalerna, Kronofogden and Lendo, among others, and we also highlight young people's own perspectives.

content.title: More moving chains, affordable building projects, future buyers — how to balance the housing market
content.description: The conditions for a balanced and growing housing market are currently lacking. High prices and poor accessibility leave many people living in homes that do not meet their needs. Greater mobility and more chains of moves in the housing market are therefore needed.
content.extendedDescription:
As the population ages, the need for housing suited to older people grows. At the same time, the barrier to young people buying their first home is rising, hampering mobility in the housing market.

The panel discusses how to create more chains of moves and a better-balanced housing market through sustainable, commercially viable solutions. The conversation focuses on how smart choices throughout a property's lifecycle, from development and construction to management, sale and moving in, can improve accessibility, lower costs and use resources better.

Who is the housing customer of the future, and whom are we actually building for? The panel also explores how future-proof building concepts can create long-term value for property owners and residents and contribute to a more sustainable, functioning housing market.

content.title: From waste to resource – making the civil engineering sector circular
content.description: Producing new materials causes far too many carbon dioxide emissions. How can we extend materials' lifespans while increasing reuse in civil engineering? What can we learn from previous generations?
content.extendedDescription: The panel begins by discussing how civil engineering can work more circularly with excavated materials, soils and organic resources. The focus is on reusing materials currently transported away or classified as waste in new projects, reducing climate impact and costs and using land more efficiently without consuming new natural resources. What role does the location of these “resource sites” play for the environment and projects? The discussion also examines how construction and civil engineering previously worked more closely with natural conditions and local resources than is often the case today, in Sweden and elsewhere. It addresses how today's built environment development affects land, agriculture and biodiversity, and the consequences for future generations. The panel highlights barriers and opportunities for reuse and how policy and regulations can support greater circularity and more sustainable development.

content.title: Who takes responsibility when systems fail? Digital resilience as a leadership issue
content.description: Sweden is digitalising faster than we are building resilience. Municipalities, regions, government agencies, businesses and civil society depend on digital systems, and no one else can guarantee delivery if those systems come under pressure or fail. We must move from digital dependence to digital resilience.
content.extendedDescription:
Hope is not a digital security strategy. Today's geopolitical situation means the likelihood of attacks on our digital systems is no longer negligible — risk and vulnerability assessments must change. An organisation providing essential services in Sweden suffers a successful cyberattack every week, and most lack a concrete plan for what happens when critical systems fail. Waiting makes no one stronger.

Netnod invites you to a panel discussion on how Sweden can move from digital dependence to digital resilience. Representatives from politics, business, the public sector and technical experts meet on stage to discuss what is actually needed for essential organisations to function when the unexpected occurs, and what action must be taken now. The discussion is open to everyone who wants to listen.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: How is shipping's transition progressing?
content.description: Reducing humanity's negative impact on the climate is one of today's greatest and most important challenges. It concerns every part of society, not least shipping. Changing shipping's energy use is a challenge requiring the involvement of multiple activities and actors.
content.extendedDescription: Global shipping currently accounts for around three per cent of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, while playing a crucial role in trade and prosperity between people, countries and continents. A transition to fossil-free, sustainable energy in shipping is therefore central to society's energy transition, including through transporting new forms of energy, supporting fossil-free infrastructure and participating in circular flows that reuse resources. However, changing shipping's energy use is a complex challenge requiring cooperation between multiple actors and activities. Taking Svensk Sjöfart's Climate Roadmap, which outlines a possible path to climate neutrality by 2050, as a starting point, participants gather over breakfast for discussion, experience-sharing and networking. During the networking breakfast, three shipping companies from different parts of the sector discuss their challenges and choices.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Do we need more businesses, or better ones?
content.description: Why do so few choose entrepreneurship when starting a business is easier than ever? How can we create security, business survival and societal value, and change young people's views of entrepreneurship?
content.extendedDescription:
Starting a business is easier than ever, yet few take the step. Does security determine our choices? Sweden has a high-quality business sector, and there is a desire to make starting a business easier. But perhaps the question is more about survival and long-term sustainability than starting up.

The seminar discusses how more companies can survive and create real value. We ask: does a company's survival have intrinsic value if it does not contribute to society? And how does running a business differ from being employed – can the gap be bridged?

We also examine young entrepreneurs' perspectives and views on security in career choices.
The seminar offers insights and practical examples for anyone wanting to understand the motivations, challenges and opportunities in today's entrepreneurship.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: The right to your own body – who takes responsibility for pupils in schools for children with intellectual disabilities?
content.description: Children and young people with intellectual disabilities face a considerably greater risk of sexual abuse than others. Yet schools often lack tools for prevention. How can we protect the most vulnerable when ambitions for teaching about bodily integrity and consent are being lowered?
content.extendedDescription:
Alarming reports reveal acute vulnerability among pupils in schools for children with intellectual disabilities: almost one in three girls has experienced sexual abuse. Despite these figures, educators report a lack of materials and methods for teaching consent, bodily integrity and relationships.

The new curriculum inquiry proposes removing these topics from schools' overarching remit. This risks ending cross-curricular work and removing headteachers' explicit responsibility. If the issue is confined to individual subjects, the continuity essential for long-term changes in attitudes will be lost.

The seminar starts from this situation and provides insight into Gymnasiebrevet, a project funded by Arvsfonden. We present work on cross-curricular materials being developed together with the target group. In a subsequent panel discussion with young people, professionals and politicians, we discuss how to create the conditions for preventing sexual abuse starting in the classroom.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Obesity — unlike other diseases?
content.description: Modern obesity care with drug treatment offers the prospect of eventually reversing the negative trend of continuous weight gain in the population and reducing serious secondary diseases, including cardiovascular conditions. But who should receive care, who should decide, and who should pay?
content.extendedDescription:
More than half of all Swedes are overweight, and one in six has obesity. The societal challenge is substantial, yet obesity is not treated like other diseases. Access to region-run obesity care is limited, and many people turn to digital healthcare providers specialising in obesity. Increasing numbers are treated with modern GLP-1 medicines and pay out of their own pocket.

How should regions organise obesity care and cooperation with external digital healthcare providers? How should primary care manage patients with obesity who are at high risk of serious illness? How is the clinical encounter affected when the patient pays for treatment? How can care become more equitable across regions and socioeconomic groups?

Breakfast is served from 08:00.

content.title: How do we reach net zero by 2045? Sweden first with a shared climate ambition for healthcare and life science
content.description: The healthcare sector accounts for around five per cent of global climate emissions. At the same time, care must remain high-quality and strengthen Sweden's life science competitiveness. How can the sector transition to net zero by 2045 without jeopardising patient safety, innovation or access to effect
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has high ambitions for both climate and medical quality. A public-private partnership bringing together actors across the healthcare value chain around a shared climate ambition – net-zero emissions by 2045 – was established in 2026. Healthcare, pharmaceutical companies, medical technology companies, pharmacies and other parts of life science depend on one another. Collaboration is therefore needed to reduce both direct and indirect emissions. The partnership prioritises actions delivering the greatest climate benefits, such as prevention, early diagnosis and effective treatment that reduces the need for resource-intensive care. It also focuses on innovation, circular material flows, reuse, reduced waste and climate-smart logistics. More resource-efficient working methods also strengthen robustness and competitiveness. We present the initiative and how more actors can join.

content.title: Obesity and working life – creating sustainable solutions for health and productivity
content.description: Obesity affects health, work capacity and the economy. The disease costs society many billions of kronor annually in lost production alone. How can sustainable solutions deliver better health, stronger work capacity and increased productivity?
content.extendedDescription: Obesity is a widespread disease affecting both people's health and society's economy. It is associated with an increased risk of conditions including type 2 diabetes, serious cardiovascular disease, liver and kidney disease, certain cancers and premature death. It often leads to sick leave and reduced work capacity. Nearly a quarter of people aged 45-64 are estimated to have obesity (BMI above 30). The seminar focuses on obesity as a societal issue at the intersection of health and working life. How does it affect sick leave and work capacity? What workplace consequences arise when treatment is absent or delayed? We discuss possible co-funded treatment models, including employer funding, insurance solutions and social outcomes contracts. How can these complement public healthcare without increasing inequality? What regulatory changes could incentivise investment in treatment for better health and work capacity?

content.title: The threat is here and now — how can Sweden strengthen defence capability and self-sufficiency?
content.description: How can Sweden rapidly increase self-sufficiency in the defence industry and strengthen defence capability? Is new legislation needed, or can we respond to the security situation faster by changing working methods within existing rules?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe's security situation has changed fundamentally. Sweden urgently needs to strengthen both its defence capability and national self-sufficiency in the defence industry. The question is no longer whether this must happen, but how quickly it can be done.

The seminar brings together representatives from business, defence and local government to discuss how Sweden can rapidly develop defence capability, its defence industry and robust infrastructure. The discussion covers establishment, permitting processes, spatial planning and cooperation between the public and private sectors.

Different perspectives are used to discuss how a regiment, a propellant factory and dual-use infrastructure can be established in practice. The question is whether legislation must change or whether there is already scope to act faster through new working methods and more efficient processes within existing rules.

content.title: How do we encourage more companies to participate in public procurement?
content.description: The public sector purchases SEK 1 100 billion annually, but many companies still find public procurement complicated, time-consuming and hard to navigate. How do we build a modern public market in which the best solutions want to compete?
content.extendedDescription:
Many companies avoid the public sector despite having solutions that could improve quality, innovation and efficiency. Procurement processes are often seen as complex, administrative and built for another era, risking reduced competition and making the public sector less attractive as a market.
As central government reforms procurement, much attention is given to excluding the wrong actors. This is important but insufficient. We must also discuss attracting the right actors: businesses that can improve public services, quality and resource use.
How do we create a more modern, data-driven public market in which more companies actually want to participate? How can transparency, simpler processes and AI reduce administration, strengthen competition and improve the use of taxpayers' money?

content.title: Falling birth rates – how do we reverse the trend? IVF, greater knowledge and egg freezing
content.description: Historically low birth rates in Sweden and the rest of the world are troubling decision-makers. The government has commissioned an inquiry to understand and reverse the trend. Involuntary childlessness affects 15–20 per cent of all couples of reproductive age. How can more people be given the opportunity to have the children they want?
content.extendedDescription:
Merck invites you to a discussion about the consequences of falling birth rates, including lower GDP and pressure on welfare systems, and how we can move from words to action to make parenthood possible for those who long for children but face involuntary childlessness.
Are political promises of more IVF attempts the solution? The discussion will also explore the role of insufficient knowledge about fertility and how treatment attempts for a sibling and subsidised egg freezing could be important pieces of the puzzle in reversing the trend.

content.title: How will Sweden cope with a crisis when our own medical technology is not even used in healthcare today?
content.description: Sweden has no shortage of medical technology solutions – quite the opposite. But too many remain pilot projects or never reach widespread use in healthcare. This is an everyday problem. In a crisis, it becomes a risk.
content.extendedDescription:
Meanwhile, we talk increasingly about preparedness, robustness and resilience. But preparedness is not built during a crisis; it is built on what already works. If we cannot implement and scale medical technology in peacetime, how will we do so when it really matters?

What political decisions are needed to change this, and who takes responsibility? Medtech4Health invites you to a panel discussion about the concrete steps Sweden needs to move from innovation to use, strengthening healthcare, preparedness and competitiveness.

The discussion draws on Medtech4Health's election platform and focuses on:
- What prevents implementation and scaling today
- How responsibility, funding and regulations can work together better
- What is needed to strengthen healthcare's ability to implement change
- How medical technology can become an integral part of Sweden

The seminar brings together political representatives and key actors from healthcare, business and academia for a pointed discussion about the way forward.

content.title: The state and capital – growth policy for Sweden
content.description: Sweden is a frontrunner with strong industry, cutting-edge research and innovative startups. But we are falling behind. Growth is too low, permitting processes too slow and capital too difficult to mobilise. We risk losing production and business operations while other countries step forward.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's investment architecture is insufficient to meet the new reality. How can Sweden better support Swedish companies that want to grow and scale up? How can the state help ensure major investments both come to and remain in Sweden? How can the state become a more active partner in creating long-term, predictable conditions, driving crucial future investments and mobilising capital?

The seminar explores how to lay the foundations for stronger Swedish competitiveness, increase investment and raise growth. This is central to Sweden's economic future. The seminar will discuss Socialdemokraterna's new growth policy, intended to make Sweden richer and put more money in ordinary people's pockets.
content.subject: Economy

content.title: If work can be done anywhere, why would anyone choose Stockholm?
content.description: The digital paradigm shift is making work increasingly independent of location. At the same time, competition for talent, companies and investment is growing. What determines which places are chosen, and what is needed to create attractive environments where people want to work, live and meet?
content.extendedDescription:
AI and technological development are changing not only working life, but also conditions for cities, offices and investment. When work can be done anywhere, new competition emerges between places. For companies, it is about where they can attract the right skills; for individuals, where they want to live; and for investors, where long-term attractiveness exists.

This places new demands on how we design cities and working environments. What makes a place relevant when physical presence can no longer be taken for granted? How is demand for offices and urban environments affected? And what is needed to create places people actually choose to spend time in?

The seminar discusses how changes in working life affect our view of place and what determines where people and companies will want to establish themselves in the future.

content.title: The right vehicle for the right task – why are we electrifying in the wrong order?
content.description: Sweden is missing its transport climate target not only because of the fuels we use, but because we drive the wrong vehicles. Swedish companies have already developed solutions. What is missing is regulation and incentives allowing energy efficiency to guide vehicle choices, not just fuel choices.
content.extendedDescription:
Clean Motion shows how matching vehicles to tasks can free up energy-system capacity and strengthen Sweden's resilience. Electrification is necessary but insufficient. Sweden will not meet its transport climate target if we keep electrifying vehicles designed for entirely different needs from their actual uses.

Much everyday urban transport involves short distances and light loads. Yet heavy vehicles are often used, causing unnecessary energy consumption thousands of times daily. The cleanest energy is energy never used, so energy efficiency must become central to transport policy.

Lightweight vehicles, preferably with integrated solar energy, can ease pressure on the electricity grid, reduce dependence on oil and imports, and contribute to a more robust society. Swedish companies have already developed solutions. A national strategy, smarter regulations and incentives enabling scale-up are now needed. The technology exists. The will exists. Political action is now required.

content.title: Experience heat stress!
content.description: Heat stress is a growing global occupational health and human rights issue. Textile workers in several of the world's largest producing countries regularly work in temperatures above 35 degrees, often without adequate protective measures. The consequences can include dehydration, dizziness, fainting and serious health risks.
content.extendedDescription:
What does it feel like to work in temperatures above 35 degrees, without ventilation, breaks or access to a cool space? Experience heat stress is an immersive experience in which visitors step directly into a textile worker's reality. Intense heat, authentic factory noise and workers' own accounts create a tangible physical experience. For a few minutes, visitors enter the reality that the climate crisis and conditions in the fashion industry create for many textile workers around the world. Afterwards, Fair Action invites you to discuss corporate responsibility, climate justice and what is needed for a just climate transition in the fashion industry.

Imperfect Industries will be there to share how circular business models can be created through reuse – without any new manufacturing. Their concept will be presented on site for anyone curious to learn more about how reuse can be scaled up in practice. Come and talk to us!
content.detail: The fashion industry is too hot
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: Online sexual violence against children – how can society meet the challenge?
content.description: Children's exposure to online sexual offences is increasing and changing rapidly. At the same time, many cases go unreported. What does children's vulnerability look like today, and how can society strengthen prevention and protection for children who are affected?
content.extendedDescription:
Online sexual violence against children is a global societal problem and one of the greatest challenges of our time for children's rights. Repeated surveys by Ecpat show that in Sweden, children and young people are more likely to have experienced multiple online sexual offences than not to have done so.

Children's and young people's experiences and voices are essential to understanding their vulnerability and designing relevant, credible and effective protection and support. Through its support services, removal of abuse material and knowledge gathering, Ecpat provides unique insight into children's circumstances. Barnombudsmannen has an ongoing assignment concerning contact channels for children who have experienced, among other things, different forms of sexual abuse – how do children seek support and protection today, and how can this be improved?

How can Sweden better meet the requirements of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Council of Europe's Lanzarote Convention regarding the prevention of child sexual abuse and the provision of protection and support for children?

content.title: What will happen in gambling policy during the next parliamentary term?
content.description: The gambling market has an annual turnover of approximately SEK 28 billion, and just over 70 per cent of Sweden's adult population has gambled at some point in the past year. What do politicians want from Swedish gambling policy?
content.extendedDescription:
Seven in ten adult Swedes gamble at some point each year, yet gambling policy receives very little attention in public debate. For many people, gambling is entertainment and provides a moment of enjoyment or relaxation, but it also has a major negative impact on the lives of a small proportion of the population.

For this gambling policy discussion, we have invited the people responsible for gambling policy from all parliamentary parties to discuss important issues ahead. How should illegal gambling be countered? How can innovation in the gambling market be encouraged? How should responsible gambling be strengthened, and how do politicians view the segmentation of the Swedish gambling market? These are some of the questions addressed.

content.title: Creating a reef on Kungliga Djurgården: a model for urban nature-based solutions
content.description: As climate change and biodiversity loss increase, nature-based solutions can become a natural part of Sweden's future societal infrastructure.
content.extendedDescription: Can nature become part of future infrastructure? After six years of research and development, LAGU shows how nature-based solutions can create habitats for fish and other species, strengthen climate adaptation and contribute to more attractive, resilient cities. Using Isbladsrevet on Djurgården and other central Stockholm waters as examples, we present practical experience of turning reused surplus stone into living habitats. The seminar discusses how municipalities, landowners and urban developers can move from pilots to large-scale application and make nature-based water infrastructure an established part of future development. A panel of politicians and experts then discusses scaling up nature-based solutions and integrating them into future urban development.

content.title: How can we win the global export battle?
content.description: Geopolitical chaos, accelerating technological development and trading conditions that change overnight are redrawing the playing field for Swedish export industries. What will it take for Sweden to remain a leading export nation, create jobs, attract investment and lay the foundations for future Swedish prosperity?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's prosperity rests on exports, innovation, technological leadership and global competitiveness. But the playing field is changing rapidly. Geopolitical tensions, new trading patterns and accelerating technological development are challenging Swedish strengths in industry, transport, telecoms and energy, while competition for investment, skills and the jobs of the future intensifies.

How can Sweden maintain its position as a leading global export nation, and what decisions must be made now?

This breakfast seminar brings together representatives of business, industry and Team Sweden to discuss how Sweden can remain a leading force for innovation and the global transition, creating jobs and building a strong Sweden.

- Which export sectors are at stake, and what does this mean for Swedish jobs and GDP?

content.title: Decision-making in an uncertain world: which futures must we prepare society for?
content.description: Major systems involving climate, conflict, energy, technology and geopolitics are changing faster than ever. Much of what affects us lies beyond our control. How do we nevertheless make decisions, and how can scenarios help build resilience and robust strategies?
content.extendedDescription:
Society often plans for one risk at a time. But disruptions are interconnected: wars and conflicts affect energy, the economy and goods flows. AI and other technological changes create new dependencies. Natural disasters, disease outbreaks and food crises cause humanitarian suffering.

The seminar explores how exploratory scenarios, stress tests, no-regrets measures and critical examination of our assumptions can support decisions under uncertainty. Perspectives from energy, humanitarian work, security and leadership in complex systems come together to discuss what is needed for robust decision-making processes in an uncertain world.

The starting point is a compound sequence in which disrupted energy supplies, humanitarian pressures and security-policy demands simultaneously confront Swedish actors with difficult choices. What assumptions underpin today's decisions? Which risks are we missing? And how can essential societal actors strengthen their ability to manage deep uncertainty and compound societal risks?

content.title: Now it concerns us – human rights in Sweden today
content.description: How can we strengthen respect for rights in Sweden, learn from European experience and contribute to future development of standards? How can we ensure human rights are more than fine words and instead essential building blocks of a living democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
For a long time, human rights and international conventions mainly inspired engagement concerning countries other than Sweden. Developments in Sweden and several other European countries in recent years mean that, in many areas, we have approached the boundaries set by our international commitments to the UN, EU and Council of Europe. The risk of human rights violations is increasing, particularly when decisions are made quickly with less regard for objections from experts and consultation bodies. Human rights protections, including the right not to be discriminated against, risk being sidelined.

States' respect for international commitments is fundamental to a rules-based world order. Fundamental freedoms and rights sustain democracy and underpin dignified lives and societal stability.

Come to listen and ask questions at a round-table discussion at Torget för mänskliga rättigheter och demokrati.

content.title: Who should make the banking market work better – customers, banks or politicians?
content.description: Many people find it difficult to influence their banking terms, and competition is described as limited. There is talk of values and trust, but this is not reflected in customers switching providers. Are we content simply to complain, or who actually bears responsibility for a functioning banking market?
content.extendedDescription:
Criticism of how the banking market works is recurrent. Customers react to what they see as unjustified interest rate changes and a lack of competition. Meanwhile, banks make different choices in their treatment of customers and their role in society. This concerns trust, responsibility and values: things that ought to have an impact in a fully functioning market.
Proposals for change exist. Customers are urged to become more active and negotiate. Politicians are proposing a bank tax. Choice and transparency are increasing, yet inertia persists.
Whose responsibility is it really? Are customers too passive, are authorities failing to fulfil their duties, or do the rules stand in the way? Who has the greatest opportunity, and responsibility, to drive progress towards a better-functioning market? Or are we actually content simply to complain?
Join politicians, authorities, banks and consumer organisations for a discussion at Landshypotek Bank.

content.title: People have different circumstances: why we need more routes to the same professional goal
content.description: More training places are not enough unless they lead to professional skills. Better course design, more accurate matching and greater understanding of individualised learning can create more routes to the same goal without lowering standards.
content.extendedDescription:
Try this. 926 characters.

Sweden needs more people with vocational skills. But more training places are not enough unless they lead all the way to employment. When people differ in experience, learning conditions and needs for pace, structure and support, education must become better targeted.

ETG College has built a unique, industry-supported adult vocational education model with two routes to the same professional goal: regular education and accelerated learning. Both feature clear structure, progression, workplace requirements and quality assurance. Capacio contributes cognitive mapping focusing on how people absorb information, handle pace, solve problems and function in different learning environments.

Together, ETG College and Capacio show how multiple pathways, better course design and greater understanding of different learning conditions can improve matching and completion and enable more people to gain employable skills without lowering standards.

content.title: Smart locks for smart homes: Why cybersecurity needs to be considered
content.description: It is often assumed that cybersecurity is an important topic for businesses, public institutions and critical infrastructure. As smart homes become increasingly popular, also certain consumer IoT devices (e.g. smart locks), could become targets of cyberattacks, possibly leading to home burglaries.
content.extendedDescription:
The media regularly reports on successful cyberattacks, many of which have caused considerable damage. However, most companies and public sector organisations have put in place appropriate technologies, processes and awareness-raising measures to protect themselves against  such attacks.
On the other hand, in their private lives, almost everyone is nowadays aware that their mobile phones, tablets and computers are vulnerable to potential attacks. What many consumers do not have on their radar, is a potential security vulnerability in smart home products.
The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), which shall fully apply from 11 December 2027, aims to safeguard businesses and consumers. As part of the implementation programme of the CRA, a harmonised European standard for “Essential cybersecurity requirements for smart home products with security functionalities” is currently prepared.
This topic will be covered in a lecture supported by slides, followed by a question-and-answer session.

content.title: Sustainable defence companies are not built on one purchase – how can SMEs grow alongside total defence?
content.description: Sweden is undertaking a historic defence build-up, while the security situation in our region is characterised by prolonged uncertainty. This places new demands on how we build strong, resilient total defence, in which small and medium-sized enterprises play a crucial role.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's defence depends on small and medium-sized enterprises, both as direct suppliers and as part of larger companies' value chains. Yet many SMEs struggle to enter the market and grow within the sector. Many find it difficult to secure continuing orders after an initial purchase, creating major barriers to growth.

If Sweden is serious about strengthening its defence capability, purchasing individual solutions is not enough. The state must create better conditions for smaller companies to develop, scale up and become integrated into total defence's long-term supply chains.

The seminar discusses the concrete changes needed: faster procurement routes, more testbeds close to Försvarsmakten's operational needs, clearer pathways from initial orders to larger contracts, better financing between prototype and scale-up, and greater responsibility for established defence companies to open their value chains to Swedish SMEs.
content.subject: Security/defence
speakerTitles: Head of the Stockholm School of Economics Center for Security & Resilience

content.title: AI in practice – how do Swedish companies create business value, competitiveness and trust?
content.description: AI is often highlighted as crucial to Sweden's future competitiveness. But how do Swedish organisations move from AI strategies and pilot projects to tangible impact in customer interactions, decision-making and service development? And how can this development also strengthen responsibility, skills and lasting trust?
content.extendedDescription:
In a short time, AI has gone from a question for the future to a crucial issue for business, working life and society. For Swedish organisations, the next step is no longer about testing the technology – it is about creating real value in their operations.

This development is about more than efficiency and innovation. It also raises broader questions about responsibility, skills and trust. How do organisations prioritise different AI investments? How do they ensure that these investments actually have an impact? And how do they build leadership, culture and self-leadership at a time when AI is rapidly changing roles, responsibilities and expectations?

At this seminar, organised by Svenska Spel and Google, perspectives from business and politics meet in a discussion about how AI. The discussion also looks ahead. Which choices will be crucial in the coming years? What will distinguish organisations that succeed from those that fall behind? And what do politicians, businesses and organisations need to do now for Sweden to remain at the forefront?
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: The Stockholm–Mälar region in the national plan — major benefits but implementation challenges
content.description: The Stockholm–Mälar region accounts for just over half of Sweden's GDP. If Mälardalsrådet's prioritised infrastructure investments are implemented, benefits could reach SEK 222 billion. But this requires projects to be completed on time and skills shortages to be addressed.
content.extendedDescription:
More than four million people live in the Stockholm–Mälar region, which is home to several global corporations. 150 million tonnes of freight are transported to, from and through the region. 850 000 residents commute across one or more municipal boundaries to get to work. 8 out of 10 train journeys in Sweden start or end in Stockholm.

A report from Mälardalsrådet shows that investment in the Stockholm–Mälar region's transport infrastructure delivers benefits of SEK 222 billion through, among other things, shorter journey times, increased freight transport, climate benefits and higher tax revenues. The benefit analysis is based on priorities for roads, railways and shipping lanes agreed by seven regions within Mälardalsrådet's transport policy cooperation En Bättre Sits.

The event is part of Mälardalsarenan, organised by Mälardalsrådet, Mälardalens universitet and Västerås stad.
