content.title: Tomorrow's industry is being built now — but who will do the work?
content.description: Sweden is undergoing its biggest industrial transformation in generations. New investments are being made, new jobs are emerging and demand for skills is exploding. Amid this industrial boom, a crucial question arises: who will do the work?
content.extendedDescription:
Industry needs technicians, engineers, operators, data analysts, project managers and leaders as large generations retire. Competition for skills is intensifying. In this situation, Sweden cannot afford to draw on only half its talent pool.

In this discussion, we explore women, skills and the green industrial revolution, using Dalarna as a concrete example of a region where Sweden's next major growth cluster is emerging. Dalarna has global industrial companies, strong innovation and substantial skills needs in energy, steel, mining and advanced manufacturing.

We ask how to bring more women into technical professions, production and management. Do we need to broaden the image of what an industrial job is today? And how can more women of all ages come to see industry as an attractive place to grow, lead and drive change?

Tomorrow's industry is being built now. Does Sweden dare to build it using everyone's skills?
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Save Sweden's deposit return system!
content.description: Sweden has one of the world's most effective deposit return systems, with high collection rates and clear climate benefits. Yet the EU's new Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR) risks changing the landscape, even in countries where systems already work well.
content.extendedDescription:
Several Nordic countries have already acted and requested exemptions from EU requirements that effectively mean returning to glass bottles in red and blue plastic crates, citing increased costs, more complex logistics and, in some cases, a risk of higher emissions. Sweden's path remains unclear.

In this panel discussion, we explore what overimplementation of the PPWR would mean in practice. What would the consequences be for Swedish breweries and retailers? Is there a risk of undermining a well-functioning system? And how have other countries, such as Norway, approached their choices?

We also raise the fundamental question: if Sweden is already a leader, what problem are we actually trying to solve?
content.subject: Business

content.title: How much should a beer be allowed to cost?
content.description: Alcohol tax is an important public health tool, but also depends on legitimacy among consumers and businesses. Where is the threshold beyond which further increases risk having the opposite effect through changing purchasing habits, cross-border shopping or reduced acceptance of the system?
content.extendedDescription:
The price of a beer is determined not just by what is in the bottle but above all by political decisions throughout the value chain. In recent years, Swedish households have seen costs rise sharply. Meanwhile, breweries face rising prices for raw materials, energy, transport and packaging.

Reasonable excise duties on beer matter. Excessively high prices risk not only harming businesses and jobs but also changing consumer behaviour, increasing cross-border shopping and illegal imports, and ultimately challenging trust in Sweden's entire alcohol model.

This seminar starts with a simple but crucial question: how much should a beer cost, and what happens when the bill becomes too high?

content.title: What healthcare do we want – and how much can it cost?
content.description: What is healthcare's ultimate purpose: to prolong life, reduce suffering or support people through life's end? And what happens to our view of humanity when medical possibilities lack clear limits?
content.extendedDescription:
This discussion brings together physician and author Fanny Nilsson and Cecilia Strömberg Wallin, host of Filosofiska rummet on Sveriges radio. Drawing on ‘Go to A&E – How Much Healthcare Can We Afford?’, awarded Natur & Kultur's prize for a debate book, they examine healthcare's ethical foundations: responsibility, dignity, continuity and boundaries.

As more conditions can be treated through specialist care, but fewer people have coordinated, continuous contact with healthcare, fundamental questions come to the fore. And why have we not embraced the most cost-effective, secure and humane part of medical science, which delivers better health outcomes, longer lives and lower healthcare costs?

content.title: Minimum Viable Sweden – what is our baseline for crisis preparedness?
content.description: Sweden currently lacks clearly defined minimum levels for supplies, infrastructure and societal functions during a crisis. What must keep working, who is responsible, and how can preparedness be built before the next crisis arrives?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces a new security situation in which supply chains and critical societal functions must work even during prolonged disruptions. Despite this, there is no shared definition of what must actually be maintained for society to keep functioning.

content.title: Resilience and competitiveness – how can we win both races?
content.description: Climate change, geopolitical uncertainty and supply-chain disruptions have increased the need for resilience. There is a risk that resilience is prioritised over growth, while Sweden, the Nordic region and Europe need stronger competitiveness. Which measures can build both resilient societies and a stronger economy?
content.extendedDescription:
Climate change, geopolitical uncertainty, disrupted supply chains and growing demands for robust energy supplies have made resilience a strategic issue for businesses and policymakers. Companies working in energy, industry, transport infrastructure and buildings play a crucial role in creating societies that can both withstand crises and compete globally.

Meanwhile, Sweden, the Nordic region and Europe face fierce global competition for investment, innovation and industrial development. Resilience initiatives risk becoming short-term responses to urgent crises that, at worst, inhibit innovation and growth. How can investment in energy, industry and infrastructure strengthen both resilience and growth? How can policymakers and businesses jointly create solutions that make the Nordic region more robust and competitive?

content.title: Net-zero emissions — what can Sweden learn from Denmark's CCS initiative?
content.description: Sweden has greater potential and higher ambitions for CCS than Denmark. How can effective policy implementation translate this into concrete expansion and contribute to the goal of net-zero emissions by 2045?
content.extendedDescription:
Denmark has quickly established itself as one of Europe's most advanced countries in carbon capture and storage (CCS), with concrete projects under implementation and clear frameworks for funding and responsibilities. A decisive factor has been its ability not just to adopt policy instruments but to implement them quickly and predictably in close cooperation with market participants. Meanwhile, Sweden has both greater technical potential and more far-reaching ambitions for CCS as a central tool for achieving net-zero emissions by 2045, particularly through bio-CCS.

We offer a brief overview of Swedish developments and share experience from Denmark: which policy decisions and implementation approaches have made a difference, how the value chain has been organised and which obstacles have had to be overcome. The focus is on what actually drives progress and how Sweden can turn its potential into large-scale delivery.

content.title: Fair charging – is electrification only for homeowners?
content.description: Apartment buildings face worse charging conditions than houses. Access to charging points is poorer, charging costs are higher and green tax deductions and other support are lacking. A house owner pays a quarter of the charging cost of an apartment household. How long is this difference sustainable?
content.extendedDescription: A large majority of electric car owners live in houses with good access to charging. A private charge point, made more affordable through a green tax deduction, enables charging at low hourly prices at night and on weekends. Meanwhile, residents of apartment buildings often have much poorer access to charging, in terms of physical access to a charging point, the cost of charging and access to government incentives. This means a house owner charges their electric car at a quarter of the cost of a household in an apartment building. Representatives of the automotive industry, property owners and residents discuss what this cost difference means when the entire population is expected to use electric cars.

content.title: The state, capital or citizens – who should fund civil society?
content.description: In public debate, civil society often appears dependent on public grants. But most resources come from the public and other private actors. What role should civil society play, and how should funding responsibility be shared between citizens, capital and the public sector?
content.extendedDescription:
A broad, independent civil society is a prerequisite for democracy, openness and free debate. It provides a platform for people to engage, take a stand or contribute. But who should help fund non-profit organisations without limiting their independence, while enabling stable, long-term operations?

Civil society encompasses everything from new initiatives and networks to faith communities, popular movements and associations with histories spanning centuries. Millions of Swedes volunteer here every week, supported by a few hundred thousand employees. So how should this diverse landscape of organisations fund itself without jeopardising independence? Does the method matter? Do the state and municipalities have a responsibility, or should citizens fund civil society? What should companies' role be? A discussion based on the report 'Staten, kapitalet och medborgaren – vem finansierar civilsamhället?' (The state, capital and citizens – who funds civil society?).

content.title: A cardiovascular plan that lasts across parliamentary terms – how do we build broad political support?
content.description: In Sweden, 2.2 million people live with cardiovascular disease, and around 30,000 Swedes die from these diseases each year. This makes cardiovascular disease both the most common chronic illness and the most common cause of death in Sweden.
content.extendedDescription: At the new policy forum Hjärtdagen 2025, a majority of parliamentary parties expressed support for a national cardiovascular plan, although not all fully agreed on its need and direction. Now that the government has tasked Socialstyrelsen with developing a national action plan to prevent and treat cardiovascular diseases, broad political consensus is crucial. It is a prerequisite for the plan to make a real difference for people living with cardiovascular disease. As part of Hjärtdagen 2026, Riksförbundet HjärtLung, in collaboration with Hjärt-Lungfonden and ten pharmaceutical and medical technology companies, is organising an Almedalen panel discussion aimed at building broad political agreement on the direction and need for the national cardiovascular plan.

content.title: The voters who decide the election: who are they and what shapes their choices?
content.description: Behind party preferences lie changes in different voter groups, geographically, demographically and ideologically. Which groups are shifting most ahead of the election, and why? Understanding these shifts is essential to interpreting public opinion and possible election outcomes.
content.extendedDescription:
Public debate often focuses on parties' polling levels. Yet elections are rarely decided by the overall figures alone, but by how different voter groups shift. Small changes among, for example, young voters, city dwellers or voters without a clear party affiliation can have a major impact on the final result.
This seminar examines in greater depth which voters actually decide elections. We look at voter flows over time, which groups are most likely to change their vote, and how patterns differ by gender, age and region. We also explore what will matter to different voter groups ahead of the election. The event takes the form of a discussion in which analyses and insights are presented and debated.

content.title: AI on drugs – how do we get AI to stop being so predictable?
content.description: Do you also think tech has become rather boring? How can we influence the way AI thinks to make the technology more creative, surprising and useful?
content.extendedDescription:
AI can write, summarise, code and improve efficiency. But how do we stop it being a bland, less-than-smart assistant? And can we make it think less like a well-behaved assistant and more like a creative colleague with unexpected ideas by taking code-based substances that open up the digital brain, just as humanity has done for thousands of years? André Frisk, Head of Tech at Geelmuyden Kiese, takes us through how to make technology think differently – and more entertainingly.

An occasionally comprehensible introduction to why AI often becomes predictable, how to steer it towards more original ideas, and what that means for creativity, innovation and working life. At the end, there is room for your most unpredictable question about AI!
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: When regulations hold things back, how can we secure innovation, competitiveness and patient safety?
content.description: When regulations go too far, they risk undermining their purpose. Patients must wait for medical technology that already exists, while Europe loses competitiveness. How can we strengthen patient safety without slowing innovation, access and development?
content.extendedDescription:
The implementation of regulations such as MDR and IVDR has created new problems: long lead times, certification bottlenecks and unclear application across EU countries. As a result, medical devices are delayed or disappear from the market, without clear evidence of proportionate gains in patient safety.

Meanwhile, pressure on healthcare is increasing and investors are hesitant about Sweden and Europe. The panel discussion starts from this tension: where do regulations add real value, and when do they instead become an obstacle? The focus is on unintended effects on competitiveness and how Sweden can challenge today's system, use its strength in collaboration and drive change towards faster, more proportionate processes. These should reward rapid adaptation to updated and new regulations, strengthen patient safety, innovation and competition, and deliver more sustainable and efficient healthcare.

No preparation is required.

content.title: Innovative food preparedness in practice
content.description: How does the public sector work with food preparedness in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Södertälje kommun has made substantial progress on food preparedness through innovative procurement and emergency stockpiles, known as the Södertälje model. During the seminar, food services director Sara Seing and Tomas Erlandsson, CEO of Nordisk Råvara, describe the work.

The seminar brings together stakeholders highlighting the importance of food preparedness. Participants include Michaela Haga (Region Stockholm), Sanna Palomaa (Region Gotland) and Lina Holmgren (Länsstyrelsen Gotland), who discuss links to national and regional food strategies.

content.title: A pain nurse at every primary care centre
content.description: One in five people lives with persistent pain, but primary care often lacks the right expertise. A pain nurse at every primary care centre could provide early support, create equitable care and reduce sick leave, mental ill health and the need for specialist care. Patients are currently passed around the healthcare system without a clear way forward.
content.extendedDescription:
One in five people in Sweden lives with persistent pain, making it one of our greatest public health challenges. Despite this, primary care, where most patients first seek help, often lacks structured pain expertise. Many primary care centres now have diabetes and asthma nurses, but no equivalent role for patients with pain.

Since the previous Almedalen, we have advocated for a pain nurse at every primary care centre. A pain nurse can contribute early assessment, continuity, patient education and coordination of care. This can reduce the risk of long-term sick leave, mental ill health and patients being passed between different healthcare contacts without clear treatment.

Stronger expertise in primary care can make care more equitable, accessible and effective for people living with pain.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: A pain nurse at every primary care centre
content.description: One in five people lives with persistent pain, but primary care often lacks the right expertise. A pain nurse at every primary care centre could provide early support, create equitable care and reduce sick leave, mental ill health and the need for specialist care. Patients are currently passed around the healthcare system without a clear way forward.
content.extendedDescription:
One in five people in Sweden lives with persistent pain, making it one of our greatest public health challenges. Despite this, primary care, where most patients first seek help, often lacks structured pain expertise. Many primary care centres now have diabetes and asthma nurses, but no equivalent role for patients with pain.

Since the previous Almedalen, we have advocated for a pain nurse at every primary care centre. A pain nurse can contribute early assessment, continuity, patient education and coordination of care. This can reduce the risk of long-term sick leave, mental ill health and patients being passed between different healthcare contacts without clear treatment.

Stronger expertise in primary care can make care more equitable, accessible and effective for people living with pain.

content.title: Advanced healthcare at home: how can better care be provided at home, and who benefits?
content.description: How can advanced healthcare at home make a difference for patients and their loved ones? Receiving care at home allows many people to remain at home rather than spending their final days in hospital.
content.extendedDescription:
Join us over two days to discuss how advanced healthcare at home (ASIH) can make a difference for patients and their loved ones. ASIH includes both care for acute illnesses from which the patient is expected to recover and care for patients with incurable illnesses, where good palliative care and symptom relief are crucial to quality of life and a sense of security. ASIH allows many patients to receive care at home despite needs that would otherwise require hospital admission.

During the two days, you can meet representatives of patient associations offering support and information to people with different diagnoses and their loved ones. You can also meet Palliativt Kunskapscentrum, which contributes extensive knowledge and experience of care, personal interaction and end-of-life issues.

Hear experiences, ask questions and discuss how home healthcare can develop to meet patients' needs in the best possible way.

content.title: A pain nurse at every primary care centre
content.description: One in five people lives with persistent pain, but primary care often lacks the right expertise. A pain nurse at every primary care centre could provide early support, create equitable care and reduce sick leave, mental ill health and the need for specialist care. Patients are currently passed around the healthcare system without a clear way forward.
content.extendedDescription:
One in five adults in Sweden lives with persistent pain. That is around 1.7 million people, with many more cases going unrecorded. Many wait years for the right diagnosis and help. Musculoskeletal pain is one of the most common causes of long-term sick leave, second only to mental ill health. The cost to society is estimated at around 2.5 per cent of GDP each year.
Behind the figures are people with fibromyalgia, hypermobility and EDS. The conditions differ, but end up in the same place: primary care, without access to staff with the right expertise in persistent pain. When help is delayed, other problems often follow. Depression, anxiety, exhaustion. Early intervention is not just about relieving pain, but about preventing an entire life from falling apart.
Two patient associations are coming together in Almedalen to move the issue from the waiting room to the decision-making table.
Come and listen to the dialogue with politicians about better care for patients with pain.

content.title: Is the most expensive food the food that never gets eaten?
content.description: We talk a lot about food prices but far too little about how much money we throw in the bin. Households account for half of Sweden's food waste. How can we reduce waste and spend the money on quality food from Swedish producers instead?
content.extendedDescription:
How much money is thrown in the bin? For a Swedish family, it amounts to thousands of kronor each year, and household food waste is a significant part of Sweden's total food-related climate impact.

The seminar brings together different perspectives on food waste at home. How has Coop Gotland reduced in-store food waste from 120 tonnes to almost zero, and what can households learn? What makes consumers choose distinctive local products over cheaper goods, and does that affect how much is actually eaten? And how can digital tools make weekly dinner planning easier for families?

There will be samples from Gotland food producers, canapés prepared by Evelina Collin Reuterfors from Sveriges Mästerkock and lunch by Millis Wernersson. The event is hosted by SmakShare, a Swedish recipe app helping families and couples collect their recipes in one place and plan weekly dinners more easily.
content.subject: Food

content.title: Beyond the headlines – how is successful social work done?
content.description: What happens when social services work with, for example, young people leaving crime, families escaping cycles of violence and homeless people accepting support from outreach services? The interventions are complex. What characterises social work when it goes well?
content.extendedDescription:
Susanna Alakoski, an author, social worker and long-standing contributor to social policy debate, “was utterly tired of hearing about failed social work”. She therefore posted an appeal on Facebook asking professionals to share cases where social services had made a difference. Around 500 responses quickly arrived, resulting in the anthology “Lyckade ärenden i socialtjänsten – socionomer berättar”. Its 24 contributors describe how they have changed lives and give a voice to a profession rarely heard when its efforts succeed.

Drawing on the book, Susanna Alakoski discusses what social work is and can be. The focus is on factors that enable success, including professional knowledge, compassion, cooperation, continuity and organisational conditions.

“The book does not seek to downplay criticism of social services; it simply wants to show that social work also succeeds. There is a profession and a skilled craft that sometimes work wonders,” says Susanna Alakoski.

content.title: Too little specialised housing for older people despite growing needs – reforms for more construction and choice
content.description: Housing can contribute to security, health and quality of life. Yet more older people find themselves staying in their homes involuntarily, experiencing loneliness, receiving more support at home and relying more on relatives. Putting people at the centre can increase care housing, but structural and financial barriers must first be removed.
content.extendedDescription:
Being able to adapt your housing to your life circumstances. Experiencing security, community and quality of life. As you grow older, you should be able to choose to remain at home, move to supported senior housing or move to care housing. But the reality is the opposite for many older people. Self-determination declines, at the cost of greater insecurity and loneliness. How did this happen? And how do we change it?
The report 'Från hinder till hem' (From barriers to homes) offers a unique examination of today's system, a patchwork of rules and conflicting funding conditions. It answers questions such as: How can more care housing and supported senior housing be built? What are the different actors' responsibilities, risks, financing and powers? How should the system for land, care payments, procurement and occupancy be organised?
Our reform agenda enables the right homes to be built in the right places, with the right conditions for care, the working environment, security and long-term operation. It is a model for greater self-determination, improved quality of life and better public finances.

content.title: China – a threat or opportunity for Swedish technology and industry? When global trade becomes local
content.description: Global trade is changing as production becomes more local. How does this affect the technology and automotive industries? What challenges and opportunities does it create for Swedish competitiveness in relation to China, the United States and Europe?
content.extendedDescription: Global trade faces its greatest transformation in decades. Geopolitical uncertainty, new trade barriers and an intense technological race focused strongly on time to market force companies to rethink. Globalisation is challenged by a new reality where new players emerge and supply chains change and become more local. How does this affect Swedish technology and automotive industries, which depend on both the Chinese market and global suppliers? What strategies are needed to navigate relations with China, the United States and Europe while strengthening Swedish competitiveness? Hear a unique panel discussion with leaders from major industrial companies Volvo Cars, Scania and Bosch, alongside supplier representatives through FKG and trade and investment promotion organisation Business Sweden. Moderator Lydia Capolicchio leads a discussion of concrete challenges, risks and new opportunities in this new era of global trade.

content.title: How Can Sweden become a Global Electrification Leader?
content.description: Can new decentralized EnergyNet systems help Sweden catch up in the climate transition while strengthening competitiveness and regional development?
content.extendedDescription:
The global transition to electrified societies is accelerating rapidly, but many countries are struggling to scale sustainable energy systems fast enough to meet climate goals and remain competitive.
This seminar explores whether decentralized EnergyNet systems — built around smart microgrids, local energy sharing and distributed renewable energy — could become an “expansion vehicle” for the transition to sustainable societies.
Special focus will be given to the emerging Energy Valley initiative around the Scandinavian Bay Area and its potential to position Sweden as a leading international hub for electrification, sustainable infrastructure and next-generation energy innovation.

The discussion explores how collaboration between universities, cities, industry and energy actors could strengthen competitiveness, attract investment and accelerate sustainable regional development.

content.title: Why are we moving less when we need it most?
content.description: In an increasingly digital world, physical activity, fresh air and meeting beyond screens and conference rooms are more important than ever.
content.extendedDescription:
During Almedalsveckan, we invite you to a relaxed morning run along Visby's beautiful shore, a way to start the day with energy, presence and good conversation. Every morning at 08:30, we invite you to a shared 30-minute jog starting and finishing at Sommarnöjen's house beside Kruttornet.

As our days become increasingly sedentary and digital, we want to create a simple opportunity to start the day with movement, fresh air and human connection. Each morning begins with a short discussion about running, wellbeing and the positive effects of regular movement on both the body and mental focus.

The pace is relaxed and sociable, and all levels are welcome. This is about starting the day with energy, inspiration and fresh perspectives together, rather than performance.

Those who do not want to run are invited to discuss the topic in the house at the same time.

content.title: When medicines change society: obesity, weight-loss treatment and the way forward
content.description: As obesity treatment changes, new questions arise about equitable access, costs, prevention and responsibility. What happens as demand rises, and how does it affect everything from healthcare and pharmacies to food, retail and consumption patterns?
content.extendedDescription:
New GLP1 medicines are revolutionising weight-loss possibilities and have already affected behaviour and consumption, particularly in the USA.

As obesity treatment changes, new questions arise about equitable access, costs, prevention and responsibility. What happens as demand rises, and how does it affect everything from healthcare and pharmacies to food, retail and consumption patterns? How do we ensure that children, young people and socioeconomically disadvantaged groups receive the support they need for prevention and treatment, and ultimately to maintain a sustainable lifestyle?

This seminar brings together perspectives from politics, public authorities, healthcare and business to discuss the way forward. How do we ensure the right patients get the right treatment? How can we afford it, and build a system that also invests in prevention and long-term outcomes? What role can, and should, pharmacies and grocery retailers play?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: From AI strategy to business value — what is needed in practice?
content.description: Why do some organisations create business value with AI while others get stuck at the pilot stage?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is high on the agenda in both politics and business, but many organisations still struggle to turn strategy and pilot projects into real use and business value.

During Almedalsveckan, Doings and Kinbergs plats 3 bring together leading voices from business, politics and AI expertise.

DISCUSSION 1. 10.15–10.35
Sweden's AI position in a global perspective
(Google, AI Sweden, Socialdemokraterna, Moderaterna & Doings)

DISCUSSION 2. 10.35–11.00
From AI strategy to business value. What is needed in practice?
(Volvo Group, Vattenfall, PWC & Doings)

11.00–11.15 Questions and dialogue

DISCUSSION 3. 11:15-11:45
AI, trust and people's everyday lives
(IKEA & Doings)

You will take away:
• Sweden's global AI position
• Why organisations get stuck and how they move forward
• How business value is created in practice
• How people and trust determine whether AI succeeds

content.title: How do the new building permit rules affect you?
content.description: New building permit rules came into force in Sweden on 1 December 2025. For many, the changes bring new opportunities – but also new questions about what actually applies in practice.
content.extendedDescription:
What will become easier to build?
What will still require a building permit?
How will Attefall houses, ancillary buildings, extensions and holiday homes be affected?
And how should we plan ahead as rules, processes and municipal interpretations change?

During Almedalsveckan, we invite you to an open discussion about the future of construction and how the new rules could affect individuals, landowners, architects, municipalities and developers.

We believe more people need to come together to discuss how to create better conditions for small-scale, sustainable construction while safeguarding quality, architecture and long-term thinking.

Drop by, share perspectives and join us and others interested in construction, community development and architecture for a discussion.

content.title: The fashion industry is too hot – who takes responsibility for heat stress?
content.description: Our clothes are sewn in factories in extreme heat – often without breaks, ventilation or access to clean water. Meanwhile, Sweden is preparing for heat stress while workers in producing countries are left unprotected. Who is responsible?
content.extendedDescription:
People in fashion industry factories work every day in temperatures above 35 degrees. The consequences are serious: dizziness, collapse and, in some cases, death. Yet production continues at a rapid pace, with pressure on prices and delivery times taking priority over a safe working environment.

Meanwhile, Sweden is preparing for increased heat risks. Employers are urged to adjust working hours, ensure ventilation and allow time for recovery. But in the countries where our clothes are made, work continues as usual, even though we share the same vulnerability to heat.

Who is responsible when the climate crisis makes working conditions dangerous in the fashion industry's global production chain, and what does a just climate transition look like in practice?

A focused panel discussion brings together perspectives from civil society, medical expertise and climate science to highlight heat stress as an occupational health issue and discuss the path towards a just climate transition in the fashion industry.

content.title: Can quality become Europe's new competitive advantage?
content.description: How can Sweden take a leading role as the EU introduces higher requirements for transparency, circularity and product data through ESPR and digital product passports? And how can the Swedish furniture industry use digitalisation to turn quality, sustainability and responsibility into competitive advantages?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe is currently reshaping the playing field for industry. With greater emphasis on circularity, transparency and digital product information, the conditions for how value is created, measured and communicated are changing.

For the Swedish furniture industry, this means not only new requirements, but also an opportunity to make existing values visible: enduring craftsmanship, sustainable material choices, high quality and responsible production.

As digital product passports and other EU initiatives emerge, the question is how these values can be translated into data, business benefits and international competitiveness.

The seminar brings together representatives of industry, standardisation, technology and the public sector to discuss how Sweden can strengthen its position in a new European industrial landscape.

content.title: From vulnerability to competitiveness: what can we learn from business resilience in the north?
content.description: The green transition coincides with an ongoing hybrid conflict in northern Sweden, where total defence, robust infrastructure and security of supply are crucial for business. What can we learn from operations in the north to strengthen preparedness and competitiveness in the rest of Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
The green transition creates major opportunities, but also new dependencies and vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, a changing security environment places greater demands on robustness, security of supply and cooperation between the public and private sectors.

In this seminar, Ramboll brings together leading players from industry, construction, transport and the public sector for a scenario-based discussion of what is needed to strengthen Sweden's preparedness and competitiveness.

The panel faces an escalating hybrid conflict in which several transport services are knocked out. How do businesses keep operating? How are business interests, social responsibility and survival prioritised when a crisis strikes? Which partnerships become crucial when systems come under pressure?

content.title: Resilience creates competitiveness – a shared direction for resilient cities of the future
content.description: When climate crises, geopolitics and disruption become everyday realities, urban resilience is crucial to competitiveness. content.extendedDescription:
Experience from Europe and the Nordic region shows that resilience is not only about managing crises. It also creates long-term growth, stability and attractiveness. Yet investment in resilience is too often treated as a cost rather than a strategic investment in the future.

The discussion draws on Ramboll's Nordic expertise and The Nordic Way report, based on round tables in Stockholm, Oslo, Copenhagen and Helsinki with 103 leaders from the public sector, property development, infrastructure, water and energy. We discuss how cities can strengthen competitiveness by encouraging stakeholders to collaborate at system level, increasing resilience to different disruptions and addressing complex societal challenges.

content.title: From words to action – co-creation across sectors for fresh thinking and results
content.description: Sweden's distinctive strengths in trust and collaboration have contributed to its development. How can we use these strengths to address important societal challenges? content.extendedDescription:

During the spring, Gaia & Vocean have gathered ideas about co-creation across sectors. At two interactive seminars in Almedalen, you are invited to develop these ideas further: how can we achieve together what none of us can solve alone?

We discuss, among other things, how to build spaces for co-creation, take responsibility in grey areas and establish shared ambitions. We explore what it takes to move from temporary partnerships to lasting, shared responsibility.

Leaders from civil society, municipalities, regions, public agencies and business will meet here. content.title: From reactive to proactive health – how do we make the transition?
content.description: Sickness absence is increasing, and mental ill health is the most common reason for long-term sick leave. Yet much ill health is preventable. How can employers, healthcare services and society work more proactively to reduce sick leave and improve employee health?
content.extendedDescription:
Sickness absence and mental ill health pose growing challenges for individuals, employers and the economy. In recent years, the costs of prolonged sick leave have risen sharply, while much ill health is considered preventable through earlier intervention.
The discussion starts from how a more preventive approach can be developed at the interface between working life and healthcare.
Occupational health services have traditionally had a preventive role, but in practice interventions often begin only after problems have arisen.

The seminar explores how employers can work more proactively with employee health, the role of cooperation between private and public healthcare, and the structural barriers that exist today. It focuses on how early interventions, better use of technology and data, and new working methods can reduce sickness absence and create more sustainable workplaces.

The event takes the form of a moderated discussion.

content.title: Healthcare supply preparedness – how do we secure access to medical supplies and medicines?
content.description: How far have the regions progressed, and what is the status of some of the many ongoing initiatives to improve preparedness for medical supplies and medicines?
content.extendedDescription:
Legislation now sets out obligations to stockpile healthcare products and for regions and municipalities to help one another when there are capacity shortages affecting the provision of certain care. Supply analyses are being conducted nationally, and guidance is available, with more on the way, on collaborating with business and incorporating preparedness into procurement and contracts.

Questions to be examined include how far we have progressed nationally and regionally in planning supplies and building emergency stockpiles of medical supplies and medicines. Is it enough to build larger stockpiles, and what happens when they run out? Do preparation needs differ between regions with different geography and populations? Should regions and municipalities also enter into supply preparedness agreements?

content.title: How do we build stronger local communities rooted in living forests?
content.description: How do we build communities where forests, local processing, the economy and people strengthen each other within the same value chain?
content.extendedDescription:
Today's construction often involves standardised solutions, long material flows, intensive timber processing and weak links between raw material origins and finished buildings. Meanwhile, demands for climate benefits, biodiversity, traceability and local resilience are increasing. Supported by the practice-oriented research project Levande skog Levande samhälle, the Rotväven building has been developed as a concrete example of how buildings can be understood as part of a larger system.
We discuss how construction can become part of a coherent system in which forests, industry, local processing and design work together. The focus is on moving from individual projects to structural change.

A short introductory film about Rotväven is followed by a panel and discussion.

content.title: From healthcare to working life – the path back through collaboration
content.description: We often speak of people as patients, on sick leave or dependent. But what happens if we instead see people as assets and future colleagues? New approaches bringing healthcare and employment services together are already being tested on Gotland – but they remain the exception rather than the norm.
content.extendedDescription:
Questions we ask in the seminar:

Why do people get stuck in systems despite labour shortages?
Do our structures prevent more people from finding work?
Is healthcare part of the solution – or part of the problem?

During the seminar, we will describe two different projects in which the employment unit and healthcare services on Gotland address these questions together, and what happens when shared perspectives and greater understanding allow us to develop a new view of patients and people experiencing exclusion.
We want to dare to challenge our own view of the 'problem' and achieve new results through shared commitment.

IPS Gotland is a project in which psychiatric services and the employment unit work to implement IPS for people with substance use disorders.

Jobbvägen Södra Gotland is part of the ESF project Gotland Forward. Employment coaches and the psychosocial team at the health centre in Hemse work as colleagues to find new ways to make a difference.

content.title: Only a fraction of children in families affected by addiction receive support – how can we do better?
content.description: 15 per cent of children in Sweden are negatively affected by a parent's excessive drinking. The consequences can be substantial both now and in adulthood. Yet only a fraction receive support. What do successful municipalities and others do?
content.extendedDescription:
Movendi has examined the support municipalities provide to children growing up in families affected by harmful substance use and addiction. The findings are presented in a report showing that support reaches only a fraction of vulnerable children. But action is possible. The report highlights examples of strengthening protective factors such as school, associations and safe adults to create a society where more children and young people enjoy safe, fulfilling childhoods.
Solutions often involve clear structures, a broad perspective, networks with associations and concrete interventions. Measures to learn from and be inspired by!

Welcome! Breakfast is served from 8.00.

content.title: Education and skills provision for total defence – from needs to implementation
content.description: Sweden's total defence faces a profoundly changed security situation. Meeting both civilian and military needs requires not only increased investment but also a sustainable long-term model for education and skills provision.
content.extendedDescription:
There are major challenges today involving inadequate coordination, varying knowledge levels and limited access to tailored training. There is also no shared platform where authorities, municipalities, regions and businesses can regularly meet, train and practise together.

Strengthening total defence's implementation capacity requires more than stronger governance and resources: it also needs new structures, approaches and a shared physical meeting place enabling practical application, collaboration and skills development across sectors.

The seminar starts from these challenges, examining how Sweden can move from strategy to concrete implementation and the role a new total defence training centre could play.

content.title: From innovation to competitiveness – how can Sweden become more attractive for R&D?
content.description: Global competition for investment in research, clinical trials and innovation is intensifying. How can Sweden become more attractive for R&D? And what role do the early use of new medicines and better treatment follow-up play in attracting life science investment?

content.title: The manager as society's shock absorber – when did leadership become the solution to everything?
content.description: More and more workplace problems are described as leadership problems, even though they are often fundamentally psychological, relational and organisational. What will be required of tomorrow's managers when their remit expands faster than the conditions needed to fulfil it?
content.extendedDescription:
Does every manager need to be a psychologist? Not at all. But managers need to understand the people they lead and have the organisational conditions to lead in a humane, sustainable way. At a time of sky-high sick leave rates, declining interest in management roles and growing anxiety about AI in working life, the question of what leadership should actually be is becoming increasingly crucial.

In this lecture, Paulina Tranfelt, a licensed psychologist specialising in leadership and organisation, challenges today's view of leadership through three questions: what is not working in contemporary leadership? Why is it not working? And above all, how can we do things differently?

The lecture offers a psychological look ahead at what is needed to build organisational health, more humane leadership in a digitalised world, and sustainable working lives in which both managers and employees can function, develop and thrive over time.

The lecture starts at 10.15 and lasts approximately 45-50 minutes. There will be an opportunity for questions afterwards.

content.title: What is happening to Gotland's water?
content.description: The water beneath our feet — the water that should simply be there, flow from the tap and work. On Gotland, that is not the case. The municipal water has been unfit for consumption, quarrying is lowering groundwater levels and groundwater is not being replenished. What needs to happen?
content.extendedDescription:
From Tuesday to Thursday, Urbergsgruppen invites you to discussions at its tent on Hamnplan.
Tuesday 23 June:
10:00 — Mia Svedäng, Svenska Naturskyddsföreningen, and Karin Bengtsson, Urbergsgruppen: a discussion on wetlands, water in agriculture, the EU Water Framework Directive and the vital importance of water.
14:00 Eva-Lotta Helsdotter, Karin Gardell and Stefan Persson — Expanded quarrying: what will the consequences be?

Wednesday 24 June:
10:00 Katarina Luhr, Member of Parliament, Lisa Wanneby, Urbergsgruppen — SGU's remit: why is water not the top priority?
14:00 Leif Pettersson from Hästnäs and Wolfgang Brunner — How long will the cement industry continue to poison Gotland's groundwater?

Thursday 25 June:
10:00 Jenna Senecal & Karin Bengtsson — How can we conserve groundwater? How can we make our water use circular?

Leif Pettersson will also lead excursions in the footsteps of Heidelberg Materials. Register your interest at our tent!

content.title: Life in displacement – what is everyday life like for those forced to leave everything behind?
content.description: What are everyday life and reality like for the people behind refugee statistics?
content.extendedDescription: In one of the refugee tents we use around the world, we explain our work and offer a concrete insight into everyday life for displaced people. The tent is built to withstand extreme heat, cold, heavy rain and strong winds. But it is more than shelter from the weather. For many families, it becomes a first step towards safety and hope for the future. UNHCR's work also goes beyond providing emergency shelter and relief. In all the more than 130 countries where we operate, we support people forced to flee war, conflict and persecution in many ways. This can mean helping families reunite, offering legal assistance and creating safety and hope so displaced people can rebuild their lives. A warm welcome to our refugee tent for an encounter with the reality behind refugee statistics.
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Municipal and regional politicians and renewable energy – what is needed to accelerate the energy transition?
content.description: Much of the energy transition happens locally, with municipalities and regions playing a crucial enabling role. Many have ambitious targets for expanding renewable energy but face challenges in putting those targets into practice.
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar brings together representatives of municipalities, regions and the energy industry to discuss what is needed to accelerate the transition. How can municipalities and regions take a more active role? What conditions must be in place to enable more energy projects? And how do we move from ambitious targets to concrete action?

The discussion focuses on solutions, from local benefits and acceptance to more efficient permitting processes and stronger partnerships, to accelerate the energy transition.
content.subject: Energy
speakerTitles: County Governor of Södermanlands län and Former Director-General of Energimyndigheten
Doctoral Researcher in Resilient Energy Systems

content.title: From the lab to life – how cancer research becomes innovation
content.description: Swedish cancer research is world-class, but many research findings never reach patients or deliver societal benefit. How can we strengthen the conditions for researchers to commercialise their findings?
content.extendedDescription: The seminar brings together researchers, civil society, business and decision-makers to discuss barriers, opportunities and concrete solutions to strengthen the commercialisation of Swedish cancer research and Sweden's competitiveness in life science.
content.subject: Research
content.organizationType: Collaboration between different types of organisation

Head of the Research and Health Department

content.title: Business plus the public sector: does that add up to more young people in work?
content.description: We cannot afford to lose a generation on its way into working life while employers are crying out for skills. Helping more people get their first job takes more than individual projects and goodwill. Business and civil society are on board; can we go further if the public sector dares to join them?
content.extendedDescription:
While many young people are far from entering the labour market, employers report growing skills shortages. This paradox affects growth, inclusion and confidence in the future, and no single actor can resolve it alone.

Despite substantial investment, many organisations still work in parallel rather than together. But the future labour market requires new ways of acting jointly across business, the public sector, education and civil society. The question is no longer whether we need to cooperate, but how to make cooperation the norm and build both a culture and structures that make a real difference to young people's pathways into work.
During the seminar, we will hear voices from parts of society where change is already happening, on how to move from short-term initiatives to shared long-term responsibility. We highlight good examples and discuss how they can be scaled up and spread.
content.subject: Employment/labour market
speakerTitles: Director of Local Labour Market Services

content.title: Who is responsible for engagement – individuals or civil society?
content.description: Civil society plays a central role in democracy, welfare and social cohesion. At the same time, forms of engagement are changing rapidly and often take the form of short-term efforts close to individuals' lives. As engagement becomes more episodic, established structures are challenged.
content.extendedDescription:
Through organised forms of engagement, civil society has created space for participation, responsibility and democratic learning over time. Membership and association life have enabled people to participate, exert influence and learn how democracy works in practice. At the same time, research shows that interest in traditional forms of engagement, such as membership, has declined, especially among younger people.
Engagement increasingly takes the form of short-term efforts close to individuals' lives rather than long-term participation. This is happening as expectations of civil society increase – to contribute to democratic participation, social cohesion and sometimes welfare provision. When giving increases but formal participation declines, collective responsibility, internal democracy and legitimate representation are challenged.
This raises crucial questions: how does engagement arise today, and whose responsibility is it to shape and sustain it? Do organisations need to change how they work to remain relevant?
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: The forest industry as an engine – how can we accelerate growth and the transition?
content.description: One of Sweden's competitive advantages is its access to forests. In the long term, global demand for biomass for fossil-free products is expected to increase. Yet the challenges facing one of Swedish business's flagship sectors are greater than they have been for many years.
content.extendedDescription:
The forest sector is one of Sweden's most important export industries and a central part of both the Swedish economy and the green transition. A unique value chain has been built around the forest – from forestry and sawmills to pulp and paper mills and the transport sector – in which every link depends on the others. Industry creates the value of the forest for forest owners, and raw materials from the forest underpin industry's competitiveness.

But conditions are tougher than they have been for a long time. Meanwhile, the long-term trend clearly points in one direction: global demand for biomass and fossil-free products will increase. The question is whether Sweden is ready to take that position.

The transition from fossil to renewable resources must continue at full strength: for the climate, preparedness and Swedish competitiveness. The forest sector is one of the industries that can deliver on all three fronts, but it requires the right conditions: a functioning value chain, stable long-term rules
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Forests of the future — which decisions today will shape society in 2100?
content.description: Forests' long rotation periods — in Sweden, trees are harvested after an average of 100 years — mean today's political decisions affect the economy, welfare, jobs, climate and biodiversity well into the next century. How should conflicting goals be balanced when future needs meet today's choices?
content.extendedDescription:
What will Sweden look like in 2100 — and what decisions must be made today to get us there? This seminar brings together representatives of political youth organisations to discuss the forests and society of the future. When welfare, rural development, consumption, climate and biodiversity are weighed against each other, what do they choose — and why?

Forests must meet many needs: jobs, exports, the climate transition, biodiversity and thriving rural areas. But when not everything can be prioritised at once, political choices become decisive.

One question is central: how do we make wise decisions about a resource whose consequences will only be felt long after the next election campaign?

This is a discussion about responsibility, direction and confidence in the future — but also about which decisions actually strengthen Sweden's raw material supply, competitiveness and welfare in the long term.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Saving and preserving kidneys – addressing the growing problem of kidney disease
content.description: Sweden faces a growing problem: chronic kidney disease is increasing, but awareness is low among both the public and primary healthcare providers. Many people remain undiagnosed for a long time and miss treatment that could slow the disease. Meanwhile, the system delays the introduction of effective new medicines.
content.extendedDescription:
The consequences are poorer quality of life for patients and substantial costs for healthcare and society. The later chronic kidney disease is detected, the greater the risk of needing dialysis or a kidney transplant to survive. Improving the situation requires earlier detection, lifestyle changes and appropriate treatment to slow progression and preserve kidney function.

The seminar launches the report “Att rädda och spara njurar – om en växande sjukdomsbörda och värdet av att bromsa kronisk njursjukdom”. It examines the disease's prevalence, medical and socioeconomic consequences, patients' circumstances, the value of treatment and the measures needed for more sustainable kidney care.

Clinical experts, patient representatives and decision-makers meet to discuss how Sweden can take a comprehensive approach to kidney health and improve patients' quality of life and prospects.

content.title: How can AI make our public-service processes more efficient? What can we learn from Norway?
content.description: How can AI improve the efficiency of public-service processes? Digitalisation of core welfare processes is accelerating, but the gap between pilots and production, and between technology and real operational value, determines whether AI becomes a powerful tool or more unfulfilled potential.
content.extendedDescription:
AI has the potential to revolutionise welfare provision, but the path from promising experiments to full-scale implementation is often obstructed. Why do so many projects get stuck in the pilot phase? What is needed for AI to deliver measurable efficiency in society's core processes? During the seminar, we look towards Norway, which has made considerable progress integrating AI into the public sector. We analyse success factors and pitfalls and discuss how Sweden can use these lessons to get started sooner. Discussion themes:
• From the lab to reality: How do we scale AI solutions to make a difference in everyday life for both citizens and employees?
• Norwegian experiences: What concrete results have been achieved in Norway, and what can we copy?
• Governance and leadership: How do we lead an organisation through a technological shift where value often arises at the intersection of IT and core operations?
Join an exchange of experience on closing the gap between technology and value.

content.title: AI, automation and the human factor – can industry manage the transition?
content.description: Industry is becoming more automated and AI-supported. Yet our ability to interpret information, prioritise and make decisions is crucial when the unexpected happens. Requirements are now increasing faster than systems develop. How can we build systems that strengthen decision-making and reduce errors and accidents?
content.extendedDescription:
Safety work has long focused on processes, technology and compliance. As systems grow more complex, employees' roles change. Safety and quality increasingly concern how information is absorbed, prioritised and translated into decisions. This involves interaction between new technologies such as AI and cognitive capacities.

In many organisations, demands on decision-making are growing faster than organisational systems develop. This creates a gap between what employees are expected to handle and the support systems actually provide. When systems and methods do not reflect cognitive capacities, the risk of incidents, accidents and costly decisions increases.

The seminar highlights examples of how companies can strengthen safety, quality and operational capability by designing technology and systems that better support decision-making in complex, automated operations.

Drawing on research, we bring researchers and businesses together to discuss what is at stake when technology develops faster than systems and working methods.
content.subject: Business

content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's pulp and paper industry is at a critical point. The trade union Pappers sees how uncertain energy policy, weak policy instruments and a lack of stable long-term rules drive up costs, hamper investment and threaten jobs. Major redundancy announcements show that the crisis is not approaching – it is already here.

Current policy does not meet industry's needs. Active industrial policy is required to create stable, predictable conditions, a prerequisite for investment in fossil-free production and new technology in Sweden.

During the seminar, Pontus Georgsson, President of Pappers, and Jonas Algers, Industrial Policy Analyst at Katalys, present three reform proposals to strengthen competitiveness, secure investment and safeguard jobs throughout the country.

A discussion between politics, civil society and business follows, on moving from short-term measures to policies that build tomorrow's industry.
